Hay unos pocos momentos en la vida de un hombre que son verdaderamente capaces de cambiarlo en lo más profundo de su ser. Ya sea a través del dolor o de la paz, de la tristeza o de la alegría. Para un fotógrafo como yo, los sentimientos que surgen a lo largo de los años se convierten gradualmente en parte de mi lenguaje fotográfico.

El momento que documento aquí es la muerte de mi hermano menor

El 9 de febrero de 2020, mi hermano, Pedro Henrique, falleció mientras luchaba contra el cáncer. Tenía solo 13 años. Al principio, sentí que había perdido toda mi motivación como fotógrafo y como individuo. Era imposible ignorar el dolor de perder a alguien a quien amaba y vivir fingiendo que todo estaba bien.

Puede parecer una exageración, pero fue la fotografía lo que me hizo volver a apreciar la vida. Tan pronto como comenzó la pandemia de Covid-19, tomé una vieja cámara analógica que tenía y decidí empezar a documentar esos momentos cotidianos del aislamiento en casa. Lo hice sin grandes pretensiones; solo intentaba reconectar con las personas y el entorno que me rodeaban. Poco a poco, la fotografía se convirtió en parte de mi proceso de duelo y sanación, y me enseñó a poner siempre sentimientos verdaderos en todo lo que hago.

There are a few moments in a man’s life that are truly capable of changing him in the depths of his being. Whether through pain or peace, sadness or joy. For a photographer like me, the feelings that arise over the years gradually become part of my photographic language.

The moment I am documenting here is my younger brother’s death

On February 9, 2020, my brother, Pedro Henrique, passed away while battling cancer. He was only 13 years old. At first, I felt that I had lost all my motivation as a photographer and individual. It was impossible to ignore the pain of losing someone I loved and live pretending everything was fine.

It may seem like an exaggeration, but it was photography that made me appreciate life again. As soon as the Covid-19 pandemic started, I took an old analog camera that I had, and decided to start documenting those ordinary moments isolated at home. I did this without having any big goals in mind; I was just trying to reconnect with the people and environment around me. Slowly, photography became part of my experience of mourning and healing, and it taught me to always put true feelings in everything I do.

Since losing my brother, my parents and I wanted to accomplish an important expedition in honor of him. In 2022, we made the pilgrimage along the Camino de Santiago de Compostela in Spain. Over 30 days, we covered almost 800km on foot, heading to the cathedral which houses the tomb of the Apostle James. We walked, we prayed, and met incredible people. I consider it one of the greatest healing and faith experiences of my life.

I documented our entire journey with a Pentax Spotmatic F, a Super Takumar 35mm f/3.5 lens and 30 rolls of color and black and white film. I knew I would run out of words to describe certain moments and scenes, so I photographed them.

I took my brother, my best friend, my adventure companion, to enjoy the forests, mountains, rivers, plains and colorful skies. All through my eyes. During all those days, I was never alone, because he was by my side. I lived every moment of this pilgrimage for both of us.

I loaded several film stocks into my camera: Kodak Colorplus 200, Gold 200, Ultramax 400 and Portra 400, ILFORD HP5 PLUS, ILFORD FP4 PLUS 125 and AGFA APX 400. Most of the time, I shot at each film’s nominal ISO, but whenever necessary, I pulled and pushed certain rolls depending on the region, climate, light, and feelings I was recording.

I can easily say that having a camera in my hand made me feel even more involved with what was going on around me. Fortunately, I had the pleasure of contemplating and photographing so many memorable landscapes and scenes. Whether it was while walking through the woods, inside an old church, or even resting in albergues, I always felt something guiding my camera. I photographed everything that seemed to deserve my attention.

I knew I would never forget the strange feeling of walking all day on the never-ending road. On the one hand, it was exhausting, but on the other, it was freeing. The truth is, day after day, I experienced a huge mix of thoughts and feelings going through my head. And that just makes it even more meaningful to me. It was necessary to really want to be there.

The entire trip was accompanied by a lot of enthusiasm and willingness, but inevitably, grief and pain were always by our side. No matter how much time passes, longing will always occupy a suffocating space in the chest. We give thanks for life but also allow ourselves to feel what we need to feel.

Other interesting reads

Many people — including friends — will never understand why we took this pilgrimage as a mission to be accomplished. One month, walking almost 25km a day, sharing a room at various albergues’ almost 9,000km from from — it really wasn’t just any trip.

I could say that our purpose was to simply visit the tomb of the Apostle James, or that we just wanted to spend some time disconnected from everyday life. But that would not be true. Placing this pilgrimage as a simple tribute to my brother is not enough either. It goes beyond that.

I can easily say that having a camera in my hand made me feel even more involved with what was going on around me […] I always felt something guiding my camera. I photographed everything that seemed to deserve my attention.

While playing a grieving cowboy, Sam Elliott once said that when you love somebody, an exchange of souls takes place. They get a piece of yours; you get a piece of theirs. But when your love dies, a little piece of you dies too. That’s why it hurts so bad… Thankfully, that little piece of them is still inside of us. So, they can use our eyes to see the world.

That’s what I did. I took my brother, my best friend, my adventure companion, to enjoy the forests, mountains, rivers, plains and colorful skies. All through my eyes. During all those days, I was never alone, because he was by my side. I lived every moment of this pilgrimage for both of us.

My photos are not supposed to be artistic or outlandish… I simply recorded everything that made me feel my brother’s presence in my heart. I wasn’t looking for beauty, but authenticity. Regardless of the setting, I like my photos to say something. It doesn’t have to be anything complex or philosophical, it can just be “hey, look, I like that”. I really don’t expect people to look at my work and think there’s something lush behind it. My photos are what they are. Records. Memoirs. A piece of me.

Just as I would in my pilgrim days, today I say Ultreia. It means “forward”, “let’s move on”, or even “hallelujah”. Completing the journey along the Camino de Santiago de Compostela does not mean that the problems in my life will end. Not even the pain of loss will go away. The journey does not end here, but there is a new chapter starting. Life must go on with even more love and meaning.

Soon, this photography project will become my first photobook and a great exhibition: Santiago de Compostela es el principio, no el final.

All my photos were developed and scanned in partnership with LabLab Analógico, one of the most important film labs in Latin America. I have enormous respect and admiration for their team. A huge and special thank you to Mariana Guerra, Vitor Leite, Maria Mion, and Alessa Berti.

Thank you for reading,

~ Gabriel

Empecé a trabajar como comisario en eventos de motor aquí en el Reino Unido hace unos diez años. Todo surgió a raíz de asistir a un evento con muy poco público en un día de septiembre extremadamente frío, ventoso y lluvioso, en el que la lluvia caía de forma horizontal y despiadada. Esperaba que las carreras me hicieran olvidar el mal tiempo, pero, en realidad, aquello fue una auténtica carrera de resistencia. Posiblemente para poner a prueba la resistencia de los aficionados que, como yo, esperábamos de pie a que los coches rodaran con parsimonia, algo que hacían en un número cada vez menor. Para los espectadores, aquello era una batalla de desgaste que se iba perdiendo poco a poco.

Apenas me había fijado en los comisarios antes de ir a Silverstone aquel fatídico día, y a menudo me preguntaba cómo se las arreglaban. Cómo habían logrado «entrar». En Silverstone, eran los únicos que parecían estar pasándoselo bien. Crucialmente, y a diferencia de mí, parecían estar vestidos adecuadamente para el clima. Y ya fuera por eso, o simplemente por ser comisarios y estar, por tanto, «dentro», disfrutaban de un cálido ambiente de bromas y camaradería.

Charlando con ellos, descubrí que cualquiera puede ser comisario y que es sorprendentemente fácil entrar. A menos, claro, que sea el final de la temporada, que era prácticamente el caso. Así que, al marzo siguiente, allí estaba yo: un comisario en prácticas.

Dando un salto adelante de diez años, y tras muchas jornadas de carreras y circuitos después, allí estaba yo, en el pit lane de Brands Hatch, en Kent, al sureste de Inglaterra.

Existen muchas especialidades dentro del comisariato, pero las principales son incidente (correr hacia un coche en llamas cuando todos los demás huyen de él) y bandera (comunicación analógica con el piloto de carreras). Y luego está la labor en el pit lane y en la parrilla de salida, que es donde ejerzo como voluntario actualmente.

De vez en cuando, me guardo disimuladamente una compacta en el bolsillo para usarla en los tiempos muertos entre las sesiones de clasificación o las carreras. La Nikon L35AF es perfecta para estas situaciones porque es completamente automática, además de rápida y angular gracias a su objetivo de 35 mm f/2.8 con diseño Sonnar. Sacarla, encuadrar, pulsar el botón y de vuelta al bolsillo. La L35AF, con su solidez reconfortante —y su forma de ladrillo—, se encarga por sí sola del enfoque, la exposición y el arrastre de la película.</
https://emulsive.org/articles/5-frames/5.clean_text: I started marshalling at motorsport events here in the UK about ten or so years ago. It followed going to a very sparsely attended event on a very cold, windy, and wet September day when the rain was horizontal and spiteful. I was hoping that the racing would take my mind off the weather, but in reality, it was an endurance race. Possibly to test the endurance of the punters like me standing around waiting for the cars to trundle around — which they did in ever-decreasing numbers. As for the spectators, it was a test of attrition slowly being lost. I’d been dimly aware of marshals before going to Silverstone that fateful day and had often wondered how they managed it. How they ‘got in’. At Silverstone they were the only people who seemed to be enjoying themselves. Crucially and unlike me, they appeared to be dressed for the weather. And either because of that, or just because they were marshals and were therefore ‘in’, were basking in warm banter and camaraderie. Chatting to them, it transpired that anyone can be a marshal, and it’s surprisingly easy to get in. Unless, of course, it’s the end of the season, which it pretty much was. So, the following March, there I was, a trainee marshal. Fast forward ten years, and many race meetings and circuits later, there I was in the pit lane at Brands Hatch, Kent, in southeast England. There are many marshalling disciplines but incident (running towards a burning car when everyone else is running away from it) and flag (analogue communication with a racing car driver ) are the main ones. And then there’s being in the pit lane and on the starting grid — which is where I currently volunteer. I occasionally sneak a point and shoot into my pocket to use in whatever downtime there is between qualifying or race sessions. The Nikon L35AF is perfect in these situations because it auto-everything, and fast and wide with its 35mm f/2.8 Sonnar design lens . Whip it out, frame the shot, press the button, and it’s back in the pocket. The reassuringly solid — and brick-like — L35AF handles focus, exposure, and film wind-on duties all by itself. My Nikon L35AF What it’s not so brilliant at is reading your mind and knowing when you want deep or shallow depth of field, and guessing where you want the focus point to be. That said, I think it does have an AF hold capability that I’ve so far failed to take advantage of. Some of these images suffer from these 1980s limitations and my inability to use the camera properly. I started marshalling at motorsport events here in the UK about ten or so years ago. It followed going to a very sparsely attended event on a very cold, windy, and wet September day when the rain was horizontal and spiteful. I was hoping that the racing would take my mind off the weather, but in reality, it was an endurance race. Possibly to test the endurance of the punters like me standing around waiting for the cars to trundle around — which they did in ever-decreasing numbers. As for the spectators, it was a test of attrition slowly being lost.

I’d been dimly aware of marshals before going to Silverstone that fateful day and had often wondered how they managed it. How they ‘got in’. At Silverstone they were the only people who seemed to be enjoying themselves. Crucially and unlike me, they appeared to be dressed for the weather. And either because of that, or just because they were marshals and were therefore ‘in’, were basking in warm banter and camaraderie.

Chatting to them, it transpired that anyone can be a marshal, and it’s surprisingly easy to get in. Unless, of course, it’s the end of the season, which it pretty much was. So, the following March, there I was, a trainee marshal.

Fast forward ten years, and many race meetings and circuits later, there I was in the pit lane at Brands Hatch, Kent, in southeast England.

There are many marshalling disciplines but incident (running towards a burning car when everyone else is running away from it) and flag (analogue communication with a racing car driver ) are the main ones. And then there’s being in the pit lane and on the starting grid — which is where I currently volunteer.

I occasionally sneak a point and shoot into my pocket to use in whatever downtime there is between qualifying or race sessions. The Nikon L35AF is perfect in these situations because it auto-everything, and fast and wide with its 35mm f/2.8 Sonnar design lens. Whip it out, frame the shot, press the button, and it’s back in the pocket. The reassuringly solid — and brick-like — L35AF handles focus, exposure, and film wind-on duties all by itself.

What it’s not so brilliant at is reading your mind and knowing when you want deep or shallow depth of field, and guessing where you want the focus point to be. That said, I think it does have an AF hold capability that I’ve so far failed to take advantage of. Some of these images suffer from these 1980s limitations and my inability to use the camera properly.

Other interesting reads

The five-element/four-group Sonnar lens is lovely and sharp; and it delivers images from the slabby little Nikon far above its lowly point-and-shoot status. The whole package is a marvel of form, function, usability, and image quality.

At the circuit, with both the pit lane and paddock doors open, there’s generally plenty of light, and of course, there’s always plenty going on. And every garage is different. And being club-level racing, there are surprisingly few people about it. Yes, some teams have a generous coterie of mechanics, friends, and family. But others are often just the driver and their mechanic. For this article, I was covering a ‘historic’ meeting for the 1960s and 70s sports racers and single-seat Formula Fords and Formula 5000s. Picture, if you can, the sights and sounds (the extraordinary noise) when you’re as close as these photos.

If you’re into motorsports and want to ‘get closer,’ then maybe give marshalling a go. Or, if you don’t fancy that, just get yourself to a club meeting and have a walk around the paddock, where you’ll find everyone friendly and accommodating. You can’t get closer unless you get behind the wheel!

All images are from a single roll of ILFORD FP4 Plus developed in 510 Pyro and scanned with a Nikon D810 and Nikkor 60mm f/2.8 AF-D macro at f/8. Converted in Negative Lab Pro. Very minimal post-processing in Adobe Lightroom.

Thanks for reading!

~ Nik

Hace unos años, buscando qué hacer durante los últimos compases de la pandemia, pasé muchísimo tiempo en internet. Creo que todos pasamos un poco más de tiempo conectados. Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat... cualquier cosa que me ayudara a matar el tiempo y a conectar con otras personas aburridas que también buscaban distraerse mientras esperábamos a que el mundo se acabara o a que el péndulo volviera a la normalidad.

Fue allí, en medio de esas divagaciones, donde descubrí dos cosas: la primera fue el amor por la fotografía instantánea. En los dos breves años que han pasado desde que empecé a explorar el mundo de la foto instantánea, he acumulado demasiadas cámaras y nunca la película suficiente para disparar con todas ellas.

¿La segunda? Encontré esqueletos de metro y medio con un descuento bastante jugoso. Saluden a Jeffrey.

Compré uno INMEDIATAMENTE y lo bauticé como Geoffrey, en honor a un antiguo personaje de internet que mis amigos y yo solíamos ver. También me prometí no confirmar jamás cómo se escribe su nombre. Tomé a mi esquelético amigo, algo de película Polaroid, mi fiel SX-70 y a un amigo real (que también tenía esqueleto). Nos aventuramos hacia el único lugar razonable al que se puede llevar un esqueleto: la playa.

Tras un breve trayecto en coche, llegamos. Recorrimos el paseo marítimo de arriba abajo buscando el rincón perfecto para mojarnos los pies. A mí el agua me pareció un poco fría, pero el gran J estaba feliz como una lombriz. Tras sufrir una herida leve (aún conservo la cicatriz del momento en que mis brazos sujetaron a mi amigo esquelético), salimos de la arena y nos adentramos en las tablas del paseo.

Resulta que quienes trabajan en la playa durante el otoño están tanto aburridos como dispuestos a tolerar una buena dosis de disparates.

A few years ago, looking for things to do in the waning of the pandemic, I spent a lot of time online. I think we all spent a little more time online. Instagram, Tik-Tok, Snapchat, whatever could help me to pass the time and connect me to fellow bored people looking to pass the time as we waited for either the world to end or the pendulum to swing back to normal.

It was there in those musings that I discovered two things: The first was a love for instant photography. In the 2 short years since I started exploring the world of the instant photograph I have acquired way too many cameras and not nearly enough film to shoot in them.

The second? I found 5-foot-tall skeletons at a pretty sharp discount. Say hello to Jeffrey.

I IMMEDIATELY purchased one and named him Geoffrey, after an old internet personality my friends and I used to watch. I also vowed to never confirm the spelling of his name. I took my skeletal friend, some Polaroid film, my trusty SX-70, and a real friend (also with a skeleton). We ventured out to the only reasonable place you take a skeleton, the beach.

After a short drive, we arrived. We paced up and down the boardwalks looking for the perfect place to dip our toes. I thought the water was a little cold, but Big J was happy as a clam. After sustaining a minor injury (I still have the scar where my arms caught my skeletal friend) we ventured out of the sand and onto the boards.

As it turns out, people who work at the beach in the fall are both bored and willing to indulge a fair amount of nonsense.

Other interesting reads

We wandered into a carousel, and since there were no lines to wait on, immediately began making use of the rides. Little J loved the horsies the best. After a few laps around the circle Geof started to get dizzy so we moved along on our seaside tour.

We stopped at a local gallery, pausing to admire the art. As it turns out, I’m not the only fan of photography in our little trio! The gallery attendant was very kind and both did not kick us out and gave Jeff a sticker to help celebrate his newfound love of art.

All this walking and occasionally being thrown/dragged made me, I mean Geoffrey, hungry. So we stopped for a perfectly normal lunch of movie theater popcorn without seeing a movie. I found our impromptu lunch quite filling, but I think Jef might have been confused about how exactly to enjoy his snack.

We started to make our way home after a long day at the beach. But of course, like any toddler, Jeofrey wanted to stop at the playground to play. We indulged his whining and briefly visited a local park. 2 swings and 3 slides later and the rain we had been hoping to avoid all day started so we man handled Geofrey back into the trunk and headed home.

If you’d like to see more of my boy J, I dedicate the whole month of October to posting pictures of him in action. It is rapidly becoming one of my favorite photographic traditions, a time to hang out with an old friend, get out and about in the world, and take some cool photos. I don’t know how we’re going to one-up last year’s adventure, but it’s a problem I look forward to solving!

~ Dylan

El título prácticamente lo dice todo, pero, como siempre, ¡el diablo está en los detalles! Empecemos por lo que es HARMAN Phoenix.

  • HARMAN Phoenix es una película negativa en color de 35 mm e ISO 200 completamente nueva que se lanza hoy a nivel mundial (1 de diciembre de 2023).
  • Es la primera película fabricada por HARMAN Photo y se produce en el Reino Unido.
  • HARMAN Phoenix se distribuye en caja comercial, viene en chasis de 36 exposiciones con código DX y su precio estimado oscilará entre los 8 y 10 USD (no oficial).
  • Se puede exponer a un IE de 100 a 400, pero los mejores resultados se obtienen a IE 200.
  • La película no posee máscara de color y cuenta con una protección antihalo limitada. Puede que no se aprecien halos resplandecientes al estilo CineStill, pero sí se notará cierta dispersión lumínica (blooming) alrededor de las fuentes de luz intensa.
  • Está catalogada como «una película experimental en color para proceso C-41» y representa el inicio del camino de HARMAN en la producción de película en color. Cabe esperar cambios a medida que el soporte evolucione en futuras versiones.

It has relatively linear reciprocity characteristics when exposed for > 1 second. If the name HARMAN rings a bell, it’s because the brand is coming to market from HARMAN technology limited, the same folks behind ILFORD and Kentmere film, paper and chemistry. The title pretty much says everything you need to know but as ever, the devil is in the detail! Let’s start with what HARMAN Phoenix is.

  • HARMAN Phoenix is a completely new 35mm ISO 200 colour negative film that’s launching worldwide today (December 1st, 2023).
  • It’s the first film manufactured by HARMAN Photo and is made in the UK.
  • HARMAN Phoenix is shipped in a retail box, comes in 36-exposure DX-coded cans and should retail for around USD$8-10 (not official).
  • It can be exposed at EI 100 – 400 but the best results are found at EI 200.
  • The film does not have masking dyes and limited anti-halation. You might not see CineStill-style glowing orbs, but you will see some blooming around bright light sources.
  • It’s labelled as “an experimental C41 colour film” and is the start of HARMAN’s journey making colour film. Expect changes as the film goes through further iterations.
  • Colour-palette wise it’s DEFINITELY got a retro vibe going on, and from what I’ve seen, doesn’t do exceptionally well with under-exposure.
  • It has relatively linear reciprocity characteristics when exposed for > 1 second.
  • If the name HARMAN rings a bell, it’s because the brand is coming to market from HARMAN technology limited, the same folks behind ILFORD and Kentmere film, paper and chemistry.

Before I get to what HARMAN Phoenix is not, here are a few sample photos courtesy of the folks at HARMAN technology, plus a couple of not so creative box and camera shots from me. Let’s start with those.

HARMAN Phoenix’s has particular scanning needs, so it’s incredibly handy that the team added a super helpful scanning guide on a variety of lab and consumer scanners in their technical datasheet (scroll down for an embedded version).

So, what is HARMAN Phoenix not?

  • It’s not made by ILFORD.
  • It’s not a rebranded film.
  • It’s not a slide film.
  • It’s not a black and white film.
  • It’s not a 120 film.
  • It’s not a “special effects” film
  • It’s not quite finished — well, that’s my take, at least.

On the last point above, I’m waiting for my own test rolls to come back from the lab but my view, based on the sample photos I’ve seen to date is that this is definitely a work in progress.

I’ve a feeling this is a film stock that will evolve over time and that we’ll see some changes finessing to its colour palette, profile and light response.

I’ll go as far as to say that I’ve no doubt we’ll see folks selling rolls in bulk on innumerable marketplaces at highly inflated prices within just a few years, in the same way as the original V1 Lomochrome Purple and Turquiose are today. I’m not saying you should do that yourself, it’s just a gut feel.

For my part, the most disappointing part of this entire release is that HARMAN shipped a colour film stock that looks so insanely fun under bright sunlight during winter time in the northern hemisphere. There’s no question about it, I’ve gotta move south for the winter.

I’ll be sharing my first review of this film after I get my test rolls back from my lab. You can expect it before Christmas.

In the meantime, thanks for reading and check out the embedded datasheet (and ~20 more photos courtesy of Matt Parry, Michelle Parr and Neil Hibbs below.

~ Em

Creating process with this camera is relaxing beacuse this camera it doesn’t get in your way — sure yes, inverted image in viewfinder is bit tricky to master but hey — this was my first film roll and I know it’s not the last one! Paired with my Nikon F3 I have some really good tools for creating photos.

Thank you for reading.

~ Antonio

Hace seis meses cambié de cámara. Decidir que necesitaba una nueva cámara de formato medio fue, para mí, una elección tan difícil como sencilla. No hace falta ser un genio para adivinar por cuál me decidí finalmente, pues después de todo aparece en el título de este artículo, pero primero, con el respeto que merece, aquí expongo un poco de contexto sobre por qué, tras muchos años, abandoné mi querida Hasselblad.

Había estado disparando con una Hasselblad 500 c/m de formato cuadrado desde 2012 y creía que sería mi compañera fotográfica de por vida. Así que, imaginen mi angustia cuando, hace un par de años, empecé a sentir una especie de frustración al usarla. Esto no tenía nada que ver con la calidad de imagen ni con la fiabilidad; era algo completamente distinto.

Con el paso de los años, a medida que mi vista se deterioraba, empecé a necesitar gafas. No era gran cosa, pero sí lo era al disparar. Al usar el visor de cintura, inicialmente componía mis tomas con las gafas puestas. Sin embargo, cuando levantaba la cámara y ajustaba el enfoque a través de la lupa, tenía que quitármelas. Luego, debía volver a ponérmelas para recomponer tras bajar la cámara. Si daba un paso o dos hacia adelante o hacia atrás, toda esa laboriosa danza se repetía. Sentía que pasaba más tiempo trasteando con mis gafas que tomando fotos. Lo que antes era una molestia menor se transformó gradualmente en una frustración genuina. Intenté solucionarlo usando un visor de prisma a nivel del ojo, lo cual parecía resolver un problema pero resaltaba otro: la ergonomía. Con ese visor acoplado a la Hasselblad, sentía que sostenía un ladrillo contra mi cara, y además uno feo. Todo esto se veía amplificado cada vez que usaba mis cámaras de 35 mm; me demostraban que poder disparar cómodamente a la altura del ojo a través de un visor era lo que quería, incluso al disparar en formato medio. Así que, tras luchar contra estos sentimientos, sentí que finalmente había llegado al final del camino con la 500c/m; era hora de considerar otra cámara.

Siempre he deseado una CONTAX 645, pero solo había una cosa que me frenaba en el pasado: el formato. Me había acostumbrado a disparar en cuadrado y pasar al 4:3 me preocupaba. Cuando una composición cuadrada funciona, realmente funciona; añádele ese toque clásico que obtienes del formato cuadrado y las fotos de 6x6 pueden ser absolutamente gloriosas. Por otro lado, las composiciones cuadradas pueden ser limitantes y a veces se sienten poco naturales, por lo que la idea de disparar vertical y horizontalmente en formato medio era lo suficientemente atractiva en este punto de mi fotografía como para no interponerse en mi decisión. Había otras razones por las que sentía que esta era la cámara adecuada para mí: aparte de un visor decente y un diseño ergonómico, también cuenta con respaldos intercambiables y muchas otras características modernas como el enfoque automático. Pero lo que realmente me hizo querer esta cámara es el objetivo Carl Zeiss Planar ƒ/2 80mm que lleva acoplado; es más, la capacidad de este objetivo para realizar hermosos retratos a máxima apertura era lo que me resultaba tan atractivo y emocionante. ¡Daba por sentado que funcionaría perfectamente cerrando el diafragma para todo mi demás trabajo!

Puede sonar un poco simplista, pero si buscas en la web, casi todo lo que ves hecho con esta cámara es fotografía de bodas y retratos nupciales con ese estilo aireado y pastel a máxima apertura. Se te perdonaría pensar que solo sirven para eso. Sin duda, deben ser buenas, porque cada día cientos de fotógrafos profesionales en todo el mundo confían en estas cámaras de más de 20 años para funcionar y producir resultados profesionales para sus clientes. Todo esto debe ser un testimonio de las cualidades de la cámara y, a pesar de su reputada fragilidad, los precios de estos equipos se han mantenido elevados desde la década de 2010. Ser propietario es, sin duda, un compromiso y un riesgo; con sus componentes electrónicos de hace 20 años, puede ser costoso y difícil de reparar. Así que, cuando conseguí la mía, seguí el consejo de mi amiga y, irónicamente dado el subtítulo de este blog, fotógrafa de bodas, Viola Tavazzani, y encontré una localmente en las mejores condiciones posibles, resistiendo, al igual que ella, la tentación de importar una desde Japón.

La reputación de la CONTAX 645 entre los fotógrafos de bodas profesionales es innegable, pero no fue diseñada solo para ese trabajo. En 1999, lo que ahora podría considerarse retrospectivamente como el principio del fin del uso masivo de la fotografía analógica profesional, Contax creó lo que posiblemente era el sistema de cámara de formato medio más avanzado del mundo. Junto con su gama de excelentes objetivos Carl Zeiss con enfoque automático, respaldos de película intercambiables con succión al vacío y una amplia gama de accesorios, se convirtió en una cámara popular para muchos fotógrafos profesionales. La CONTAX 645 siempre fue un sistema profesional de gama alta, así que, cuando Kyocera puso fin a la marca CONTAX solo seis años después de su introducción en 2005, nació una leyenda.

Tras haber usado la cámara durante algunos meses, la única palabra que usaría para describirla es: Rápida. Creo que esta debió ser una de las principales filosofías de diseño detrás de su concepción. https://emulsive.org/articles/the-contax.clean_text: Six months ago I changed cameras. Deciding that I needed a new medium format camera was for me, both a difficult and easy choice. There are no prizes for guessing what I eventually went for, it is after all in the title of this post, but first with the appropriate level of respect, here is a bit of background as to why, after many years I gave up my beloved Hasselblad camera. I had been shooting with a square format Hasselblad 500 c/m since 2012 and I believed it would be my lifelong photographic companion. So, imagine my distress when a couple of years ago, I started feeling a sort of shooting frustration when using it. This wasn’t related to image quality or reliability; it was something else entirely. Contax 645 – Cover Over the years as my eyesight deteriorated, I found myself needing to wear glasses. No big deal, but it kind of was when shooting. Using the waist-level finder, initially, I composed my shots with my glasses on. However, when I lifted the camera and adjusted focus through the magnifying loupe, my glasses had to come off. Then, I had to put them back on to recompose after lowering the camera. Taking a step or two back or forward, and the whole laborious dance was repeated. I felt that I was spending more time fiddling with my glasses than taking photos. What was once a minor annoyance gradually transformed into a genuine frustration. I attempted a solution by using an eye-level prism finder, which seemed to resolve one problem but highlighted another: ergonomics. With the viewfinder attached to the Hasselblad, it felt like I was holding a brick against my face and an ugly one too. All of this was only amplified each time I used my 35mm cameras; they showed me that being able to shoot comfortably at eye level through a viewfinder was what I wanted, even when shooting medium format. So, after fighting these feelings I felt I had finally reached the end of the road with the 500c/m; it was time to consider another camera. I’ve always hankered after a CONTAX 645 there had only been one thing stopping me in the past, format. I had become used to shooting squares and going to 4:3 concerned me. When a square composition works it really works, add that classic feel you get from square format and 6×6 photos can be absolutely glorious. On the flip side, square compositions can be compositionally limiting and sometimes feel unnatural and so the idea of shooting vertically and horizontally in medium format was just about attractive enough at this point in my photography for it not to stand in the way of my decision. There were other reasons that I felt this was the right camera for me, quite apart from a proper viewfinder and ergonomic design it also has interchangeable backs and lots of other modern features like autofocus. But really what made me want this camera is the Carl Zeiss Planer ƒ2 80mm lens that is attached to it, moreover this lens’s ability to make beautiful portraits wide open that was so attractive and exciting. I took it for granted that it would work stopped down for all my other work! That might sound a little glib, but look on the web and nearly everything you see from this camera is wide open breezy pastel wedding photography and wedding portraiture. You would be forgiven for thinking that’s all they are good for. For sure, they must be good, because each day hundreds of pro photographers worldwide put their trust in these 20+ year-old cameras to function and produce professional results for their clients. All this must be a testament to the camera’s qualities and despite its disputed reputation for being delicate the prices of these cameras have since the 2010s always been elevated. Ownership is certainly a commitment and risk; with its 20-year-old electronics, it can be expensive and difficult to repair. So, when I got mine, I took my friend, and ironically given the sub title of this blog post, wedding photographer, Viola Tavazzani’s advice, and found one locally in the best condition possible, like her, resisting the temptation of importing one from Japan. Contax 645 – Front The CONTAX 645’s reputation among professional wedding photographers is undeniable, but it was not just designed to do that job. Back in 1999, what now could retrospectively be considered the beginning of the end of mass professional film photography use, Contax made what was arguably the world’s most advanced medium format film camera system. Together with its range of excellent Carl Zeiss autofocus lenses, interchangeable vacuum film backs, and extensive accessories, it became a popular camera for many professional photographers. The CONTAX 645 was always a high-end professional system, so, when Kyocera pulled the plug on the CONTAX brand only six years after its introduction in 2005, a legend was born. Having used the camera now for some months the one word I would use to describe it is – Fast.  I think this must have been one of the main design philosophies behind its conception. Unlike other medium format cameras, the CONTAX 645 has autofocus lenses, automatic film advance and wind-on as well as interchangeable backs for swapping film stock mid-shoot, replacing a finished roll can also be achieved even more quickly by simply opening the back, ejecting and loading a new pre-loaded film magazine. Add to this the bright viewfinder and great ergonomics with its main control dials gathered together above the comfortable grip that makes handling and using this balanced camera straightforward. Other interesting reads Ultreia: Making pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela 5 Frames… In the pits at Brands Hatch motor racing circuit on FP4 PLUS (35mm format / EI 125 / Nikon L35AF) – by Nik Stanbridge THE BODY The CONTAX 645 has a lightweight high-strength copper silumin alloy chassis, the outer body is clad in a hard satin black plastic with a rubberised covering on the grip area. This is where the 2CR5 battery is housed. Each battery is good for between 14-16 rolls of film. It’s a good idea to carry a spare battery because although there is a low battery warning feature in my experience it dies with very little warning. Rather than LCD panels the design uses traditional dials, each turn with a positive click and are dressed with Contax’s typical pyramid textured grip. The 645’s top plate layout has the speed control, exposure control, exposure compensation dial and shutter all together above the grip. There are all the usual flash photography features, which I’m not going to delve into mainly because I don’t use flash! Other controls such as mirror-up, DoF preview and drive mode are on the body. On the back of the grip within thumb reach is the focus control, a rotary switch with a central button. I use it in M manual mode by pressing the button to autofocus but it is possible to use S single autofocus or C continuous autofocus both controlled by a half depression of the shutter button. Focus confirmation is confirmed with a solid green • in the viewfinder and any fine-tuning of focus can always be achieved by turning the focus ring on the lens as well. The body houses a vertical-travel metal focal plane shutter that operates between 8 seconds and 1/4000 of a second. Used in aperture or shutter-speed priority it goes down as low as 32 seconds. At the top of the body is the removable focusing screen, with mine being the standard MFS-2 full matte. There is a central circle to indicate the spot meter area that appears within a rectangle that shows the focusing area, the screen is bright and final focus is easy to see. There are two other screens available with the system a split micro prism and a grid screen. The body also exposes reference data along the film rebate edge on the right side of each frame, this data includes frame number, aperture value, shutter speed, mode, lens and film type. I really like this analogue ‘metadata’ feature that permanently records information on the film, in particular the aperture and speed information of each frame. Contax 645 – Right Contax 645 – Left THE BACK The standard back on the CONTAX 645 has all the usual features of a modular system camera, a counter, ISO dial, multi-exposure lever and a slot for safe storage of the dark slide.  As well as the standard back a rare Polaroid back was also available and of course, several digital backs were made by various manufacturers such as Sinar and Phase One. Although eye-wateringly expensive these old digital backs are still available on the used market and they offer an intriguing alternative capture method to film, one that I would love to maybe try one day. The back connects to the body with a slightly awkward twist and push button that unlike any of the other buttons and switches on the camera never feels quite right. Having said that, unless you are changing film type mid-shoot removing the holder body completely is not required to change film. At the rear of the back, there is a door that flips down to gain access to the film magazine. There are two types of magazines for the 645 and both are familiar to any photographer who has used this type of system camera before with little of note. Unfortunately, the vacuum back version, which uses the same ceramic based technology as the RTS III camera is limited to 220 film only, which is regrettably no longer available. Having said that, both magazines are easy to load with film and are well-made locating into the holder with a satisfyingly positive click. Once in the holder, a press of the shutter and the motor winds the film to the first frame and each frame thereafter. In continuous drive, the motor can advance up to 1.6 frames a second. Finally, after frame 16 the motors winds the remaining portion of the roll ready for removal. THE VIEWFINDER For me, this element of the design is probably the most attractive part of the camera. It sort of reminds me of H.R Giger’s Alien head but without the jaws. Long and sweeping back it is made from the same material as the body. The prism finder is elegant and distinctive with CONTAX embossed across its low front. On top is the flash shoe and a switch to swap between centre weighted and spot metering. There is a built-in +1 to -2 diopter control and an eyepiece shutter switch to stop stray light on long exposures. The eyepiece rubber is wide and comfortable. The screen has a magnification of 0.8% with a 95% field of view. Below the screen in green LED are the battery warning, exposure counter, meter mark, flash mark, focus confirmation dot, aperture value, shutter speed and exposure meter strip. As well as the MF-1 prism finder the CONTAX 645 can be fitted with the MF-2 waist-level finder. Obviously, given my reasons for wanting a 645, I have the MF-1 and it’s my favourite part of my camera except for the lens. Contax 645 – Front Right THE LENS Okay, so this has got to be the best part of the camera and it looks like I’m not alone in saying that. I even read somewhere that ‘were it not for this lens nobody would put up with that body’. I don’t agree but I get what the writer was trying to say. The standard Carl Zeiss Planar T* 80mm ƒ2 is undeniably the best lens I have ever shot. Once again I’m not alone in feeling this way about it and like most other photographers who have used one it’s for the same reasons, plus a couple of my own. Look! If you have read about this camera before then you know all about the lens’s capacity to shoot sharp photos wide open at ƒ2 and how it makes painterly portraits each subject standing out with beautiful 3D separation from dreamy backgrounds. Not to mention all that stuff about wonderful bokeh. Yep, it does all that and it’s impressive for sure, so impressive a whole industry uses it as a signature look, but that’s another story. However, there are some other features that this lens also has that make it special, it renders contrast and tone really well with both excellent highlights and shadow detail. It handles colour and clarity superbly too, that and it’s straight as well, when shooting buildings and lines I have noticed very little distortion. I mentioned earlier that I took for granted the lens’s ability to perform well stopped down after all shooting urban landscapes at ƒ2 is not ideal. If this lens is sharp at ƒ2 then it is razor sharp at higher apertures, I’ve been perfectly happy at ƒ8 – ƒ16 with beautiful scans of city scenes easily satisfying my topographic dreams. But for me, it’s the combination of an undeniably brilliant lens and the camera itself. Being able to shoot comfortably face to face to my subject with autofocus at whatever depth of field I choose, combined with a design that is as modern as you can get with film has left me in little doubt that this change of camera was the right decision. Six months ago I changed cameras. Deciding that I needed a new medium format camera was for me, both a difficult and easy choice. There are no prizes for guessing what I eventually went for, it is after all in the title of this post, but first with the appropriate level of respect, here is a bit of background as to why, after many years I gave up my beloved Hasselblad camera.

I had been shooting with a square format Hasselblad 500 c/m since 2012 and I believed it would be my lifelong photographic companion. So, imagine my distress when a couple of years ago, I started feeling a sort of shooting frustration when using it. This wasn’t related to image quality or reliability; it was something else entirely.

Over the years as my eyesight deteriorated, I found myself needing to wear glasses. No big deal, but it kind of was when shooting. Using the waist-level finder, initially, I composed my shots with my glasses on. However, when I lifted the camera and adjusted focus through the magnifying loupe, my glasses had to come off. Then, I had to put them back on to recompose after lowering the camera. Taking a step or two back or forward, and the whole laborious dance was repeated. I felt that I was spending more time fiddling with my glasses than taking photos. What was once a minor annoyance gradually transformed into a genuine frustration. I attempted a solution by using an eye-level prism finder, which seemed to resolve one problem but highlighted another: ergonomics. With the viewfinder attached to the Hasselblad, it felt like I was holding a brick against my face and an ugly one too. All of this was only amplified each time I used my 35mm cameras; they showed me that being able to shoot comfortably at eye level through a viewfinder was what I wanted, even when shooting medium format. So, after fighting these feelings I felt I had finally reached the end of the road with the 500c/m; it was time to consider another camera.

I’ve always hankered after a CONTAX 645 there had only been one thing stopping me in the past, format. I had become used to shooting squares and going to 4:3 concerned me. When a square composition works it really works, add that classic feel you get from square format and 6×6 photos can be absolutely glorious. On the flip side, square compositions can be compositionally limiting and sometimes feel unnatural and so the idea of shooting vertically and horizontally in medium format was just about attractive enough at this point in my photography for it not to stand in the way of my decision. There were other reasons that I felt this was the right camera for me, quite apart from a proper viewfinder and ergonomic design it also has interchangeable backs and lots of other modern features like autofocus. But really what made me want this camera is the Carl Zeiss Planer ƒ2 80mm lens that is attached to it, moreover this lens’s ability to make beautiful portraits wide open that was so attractive and exciting. I took it for granted that it would work stopped down for all my other work!

That might sound a little glib, but look on the web and nearly everything you see from this camera is wide open breezy pastel wedding photography and wedding portraiture. You would be forgiven for thinking that’s all they are good for. For sure, they must be good, because each day hundreds of pro photographers worldwide put their trust in these 20+ year-old cameras to function and produce professional results for their clients. All this must be a testament to the camera’s qualities and despite its disputed reputation for being delicate the prices of these cameras have since the 2010s always been elevated. Ownership is certainly a commitment and risk; with its 20-year-old electronics, it can be expensive and difficult to repair. So, when I got mine, I took my friend, and ironically given the sub title of this blog post, wedding photographer, Viola Tavazzani’s advice, and found one locally in the best condition possible, like her, resisting the temptation of importing one from Japan.

The CONTAX 645’s reputation among professional wedding photographers is undeniable, but it was not just designed to do that job. Back in 1999, what now could retrospectively be considered the beginning of the end of mass professional film photography use, Contax made what was arguably the world’s most advanced medium format film camera system. Together with its range of excellent Carl Zeiss autofocus lenses, interchangeable vacuum film backs, and extensive accessories, it became a popular camera for many professional photographers. The CONTAX 645 was always a high-end professional system, so, when Kyocera pulled the plug on the CONTAX brand only six years after its introduction in 2005, a legend was born.

Having used the camera now for some months the one word I would use to describe it is – Fast.  I think this must have been one of the main design philosophies behind its conception. Unlike other medium format cameras, the CONTAX 645 has autofocus lenses, automatic film advance and wind-on as well as interchangeable backs for swapping film stock mid-shoot, replacing a finished roll can also be achieved even more quickly by simply opening the back, ejecting and loading a new pre-loaded film magazine. Add to this the bright viewfinder and great ergonomics with its main control dials gathered together above the comfortable grip that makes handling and using this balanced camera straightforward.

Other interesting reads

THE BODY

The CONTAX 645 has a lightweight high-strength copper silumin alloy chassis, the outer body is clad in a hard satin black plastic with a rubberised covering on the grip area. This is where the 2CR5 battery is housed. Each battery is good for between 14-16 rolls of film. It’s a good idea to carry a spare battery because although there is a low battery warning feature in my experience it dies with very little warning. Rather than LCD panels the design uses traditional dials, each turn with a positive click and are dressed with Contax’s typical pyramid textured grip. The 645’s top plate layout has the speed control, exposure control, exposure compensation dial and shutter all together above the grip. There are all the usual flash photography features, which I’m not going to delve into mainly because I don’t use flash! Other controls such as mirror-up, DoF preview and drive mode are on the body. On the back of the grip within thumb reach is the focus control, a rotary switch with a central button. I use it in M manual mode by pressing the button to autofocus but it is possible to use S single autofocus or C continuous autofocus both controlled by a half depression of the shutter button. Focus confirmation is confirmed with a solid green • in the viewfinder and any fine-tuning of focus can always be achieved by turning the focus ring on the lens as well. The body houses a vertical-travel metal focal plane shutter that operates between 8 seconds and 1/4000 of a second. Used in aperture or shutter-speed priority it goes down as low as 32 seconds. At the top of the body is the removable focusing screen, with mine being the standard MFS-2 full matte. There is a central circle to indicate the spot meter area that appears within a rectangle that shows the focusing area, the screen is bright and final focus is easy to see. There are two other screens available with the system a split micro prism and a grid screen. The body also exposes reference data along the film rebate edge on the right side of each frame, this data includes frame number, aperture value, shutter speed, mode, lens and film type. I really like this analogue ‘metadata’ feature that permanently records information on the film, in particular the aperture and speed information of each frame.

THE BACK

The standard back on the CONTAX 645 has all the usual features of a modular system camera, a counter, ISO dial, multi-exposure lever and a slot for safe storage of the dark slide.  As well as the standard back a rare Polaroid back was also available and of course, several digital backs were made by various manufacturers such as Sinar and Phase One. Although eye-wateringly expensive these old digital backs are still available on the used market and they offer an intriguing alternative capture method to film, one that I would love to maybe try one day. The back connects to the body with a slightly awkward twist and push button that unlike any of the other buttons and switches on the camera never feels quite right. Having said that, unless you are changing film type mid-shoot removing the holder body completely is not required to change film. At the rear of the back, there is a door that flips down to gain access to the film magazine. There are two types of magazines for the 645 and both are familiar to any photographer who has used this type of system camera before with little of note. Unfortunately, the vacuum back version, which uses the same ceramic based technology as the RTS III camera is limited to 220 film only, which is regrettably no longer available. Having said that, both magazines are easy to load with film and are well-made locating into the holder with a satisfyingly positive click. Once in the holder, a press of the shutter and the motor winds the film to the first frame and each frame thereafter. In continuous drive, the motor can advance up to 1.6 frames a second. Finally, after frame 16 the motors winds the remaining portion of the roll ready for removal.

THE VIEWFINDER

For me, this element of the design is probably the most attractive part of the camera. It sort of reminds me of H.R Giger’s Alien head but without the jaws. Long and sweeping back it is made from the same material as the body. The prism finder is elegant and distinctive with CONTAX embossed across its low front. On top is the flash shoe and a switch to swap between centre weighted and spot metering. There is a built-in +1 to -2 diopter control and an eyepiece shutter switch to stop stray light on long exposures. The eyepiece rubber is wide and comfortable. The screen has a magnification of 0.8% with a 95% field of view. Below the screen in green LED are the battery warning, exposure counter, meter mark, flash mark, focus confirmation dot, aperture value, shutter speed and exposure meter strip. As well as the MF-1 prism finder the CONTAX 645 can be fitted with the MF-2 waist-level finder. Obviously, given my reasons for wanting a 645, I have the MF-1 and it’s my favourite part of my camera except for the lens.

THE LENS

Okay, so this has got to be the best part of the camera and it looks like I’m not alone in saying that. I even read somewhere that ‘were it not for this lens nobody would put up with that body’. I don’t agree but I get what the writer was trying to say. The standard Carl Zeiss Planar T* 80mm ƒ2 is undeniably the best lens I have ever shot. Once again I’m not alone in feeling this way about it and like most other photographers who have used one it’s for the same reasons, plus a couple of my own. Look! If you have read about this camera before then you know all about the lens’s capacity to shoot sharp photos wide open at ƒ2 and how it makes painterly portraits each subject standing out with beautiful 3D separation from dreamy backgrounds. Not to mention all that stuff about wonderful bokeh. Yep, it does all that and it’s impressive for sure, so impressive a whole industry uses it as a signature look, but that’s another story. However, there are some other features that this lens also has that make it special, it renders contrast and tone really well with both excellent highlights and shadow detail. It handles colour and clarity superbly too, that and it’s straight as well, when shooting buildings and lines I have noticed very little distortion. I mentioned earlier that I took for granted the lens’s ability to perform well stopped down after all shooting urban landscapes at ƒ2 is not ideal. If this lens is sharp at ƒ2 then it is razor sharp at higher apertures, I’ve been perfectly happy at ƒ8 – ƒ16 with beautiful scans of city scenes easily satisfying my topographic dreams.

But for me, it’s the combination of an undeniably brilliant lens and the camera itself. Being able to shoot comfortably face to face to my subject with autofocus at whatever depth of field I choose, combined with a design that is as modern as you can get with film has left me in little doubt that this change of camera was the right decision.

¡Bienvenidos a la 9.ª edición anual del Santa Secreto de EMULSIVE, el intercambio de regalos de fotografía analógica y tradicional! El plazo de inscripción para este año estará abierto hasta el 19 de noviembre de 2023. Un agradecimiento enorme a los cerca de 650 participantes de más de 50 países que se unieron para formar parte del 8.º Santa Secreto anual de EMULSIVE en 2022. Fue un evento singular tras un par de años aún más extraños, pero me alegra haberlo llevado a cabo y haber visto los detalles tan personales que se compartieron en las redes sociales.

Con el evento de 2023, nuestra sede principal (Twitter / X) de los últimos 8 años se siente un poco inestable. Este año intentaremos diversificar un poco más las plataformas y, estés donde estés, deberías poder ver y utilizar el hashtag #EMULSIVEsanta para seguir el rastro de todo lo que ocurre en tu rincón de internet.

Si participaste en alguno de los ocho eventos anteriores, revisa tu correo electrónico ahora para ver la invitación. Si no es así, consulta los detalles y la hoja de inscripción de este año al pie de la página.

Esto es lo que cubriremos en este artículo:

  1. Para nuevos participantes: ¿Qué es el Santa Secreto de EMULSIVE?
  2. Cronograma del evento y patrocinadores
  3. Emparejamientos y listas de deseos
  4. Unas palabras sobre sanciones internacionales y otros desafíos

  6. No seas esa clase de persona

  10. Avisos legales y términos

Para nuevos participantes: ¿Qué es el Santa Secreto de EMULSIVE?

El Santa Secreto de EMULSIVE es el mayor intercambio anual de regalos de fotografía analógica y tradicional del mundo, y ya va por su novena edición.

Funciona exactamente igual que el Santa Secreto típico que podrías jugar con tu familia, amigos o en el trabajo, pero centrado exclusivamente en la fotografía analógica y tradicional.

El nombre de cada persona se mete en un sombrero y se empareja al azar con otro participante, a quien deberá enviar un regalo con un valor mínimo de 20 dólares estadounidenses (sin incluir los gastos de envío).

Cada participante termina con una pareja, y el intercambio de regalos fluye en un círculo imaginario. No es una pareja recíproca; no le estás dando un regalo a la misma persona que te lo está comprando a ti.

Imagina esto:

Cronograma del evento y patrocinadores

El plazo de inscripción está abierto desde hoy, lunes 23 de octubre de 2023, hasta el domingo 19 de noviembre de 2023. Me temo que no habrá excepciones.

Está previsto que los emparejamientos se completen durante la semana del 20 de noviembre, y los participantes recibirán los datos de la persona a la que deben enviar el regalo en algún momento de esa semana. Para obtener actualizaciones, sigue el canal oficial en Twitter/X: @EMULSIVEsanta.

La fecha límite sugerida para enviar los regalos es, a más tardar, el lunes 4 de diciembre de 2023. Como en años anteriores, dada la presión sobre los sistemas postales globales, cuanto antes compres y envíes, mejor.

En cuanto a los patrocinadores, anunciaremos algunos a su debido tiempo. Por ahora, seré breve, algo que probablemente entenderás que es un reto para mí.

Emparejamientos y listas de deseos

Ten en cuenta que, dependiendo de tu respuesta al evento, es muy posible que la persona a la que te toque enviar un regalo se encuentre en un país distinto al tuyo.

Ten presente que, si decides no realizar envíos internacionales pero eres la única persona de tu país en unirse al evento, se te emparejará para enviar un regalo a alguien en otro país. ¡Puedes evitar esto invitando a tus amigos, tanto físicos como virtuales!

Unas palabras sobre sanciones internacionales y otros desafíos

Es imposible organizar este evento e ignorar el espectro de las sanciones internacionales y los desafíos derivados de los conflictos que desplazan a miembros de nuestra comunidad global. Al igual que el año pasado, emparejaremos a los participantes rusos, junto con los de otros países afectados, con otros participantes del mismo país. Por ejemplo, si resides en Rusia, solo se te emparejará con otros participantes en Rusia.

Al igual que el resto del mundo, tampoco estamos seguros de cómo se desarrollarán las cosas en Oriente Medio en este momento. Por ahora, dejaremos que los participantes en Israel, Palestina, Líbano y los países circundantes utilicen su propio criterio para decidir si desean participar.

Envío y recepción de regalos

El "Secreto" en "Santa Secreto" significa que no sabes quién te está enviando un regalo... pero, como cada año, les pedimos a todos que le hagan saber a su pareja quiénes son en la tarjeta o en una nota junto con el regalo.

Si prefieres mantener el anonimato, es tu prerrogativa, pero ahora más que nunca, se trata de crear y mantener esas conexiones.

¡No dejes que la falta de envoltorios te preocupe! Por favor, siéntete libre de tomar una foto de lo que vas a enviar y publicarla en las redes sociales junto con el hashtag #EMULSIVEsanta. También puedes etiquetar a EMULSIVEfilm en Twitter/X, Instagram y Facebook, así como a EMULSIVEsanta en Twitter. También existe el grupo de Facebook Film Photography Chat.

¿No utilizas esas plataformas? ¡No pasa nada! Por favor, utiliza el hashtag #EMULSIVEsanta dondequiera que puedas 🙏

Sobre la recepción de regalos...

Por favor, por favor, por favor, no abras tu regalo antes del día de Navidad. Cuando finalmente lo hagas, toma una foto etiquetando las cuentas mencionadas anteriormente y usando el hashtag #EMULSIVEsanta, así como en cualquier otro lugar de las redes sociales.

Cuando llegue el día de Navidad, publica una foto de tu regalo abierto en las redes sociales y, si tu Santa te ha revelado quién es, adelante, etiquétalo.

A huge thank you to the 650-ish players in over 50 countries who came together to participate in 2022’s 8th annual EMULSIVE Santa . It was a strange event following an even stranger couple of years , but I’m still glad for it, and the very personal touches I saw being shared on social media. With 2023’s event, our main home (Twitter / X) for the past 8 years is feeling more than a little wobbly. We’re going to try and spread things around a bit more this year and wherever you are, you should be able to see and use the #EMULSIVEsanta hashtag to keep track of things in your corner of the internet. If you participated in any of the eight previous events , please check your email now for an invite. If not, check this year’s details and sign up sheet at the foot of the page. Here’s what’s covered in this article: For new players: What is EMULSIVE Santa? Event timeline and sponsors Matching and wish lists A word on international sanctions and other challenges Sending and receiving gifts Don't be one of those people How to get involved It's over to you Register for EMULSIVE Santa 2023 Disclaimers and terms For new players: What is EMULSIVE Santa? EMULSIVE Santa is the world’s largest annualfilm/traditional photography gift exchange and is now in its 9th year. It works just like a typical Secret Santa that you might play with your family, friends, or at work but is focused purely on film and traditional photography. Everyone’s name goes into a hat, and each person is matched randomly with another player, to whom they must send a gift worth at least US$20 (not including shipping). Each player ends up with a match, and gift-giving goes around in an imaginary circle. It’s not a pairing, you are not giving a gift to the person who is buying you one. Imagine this: EMULSIVE Secret Santa – How it works Event timeline and sponsors Registration is open from today, Monday October 23rd, 2023  until Sunday, November 19th, 2023 . No exceptions, I’m afraid. Player matching is planned to be completed during the week of November 20th and players will receive details of the person they’re matched to send a gift to sometime during that week. For updates, follow the official feed over on Twitter/X: @EMULSIVEsanta . The suggested deadline for sending gifts out is  Monday December 4th, 2023 at the very latest. As with previous years, given the pressure on our global postal systems, the earlier you shop and ship, the better. Regarding sponsors, we’ll have a few to announce in due course. For now, I’m keeping this quick, which you’ll probably appreciate is a challenge for me. Matching and wish lists Please be aware that depending on your event RSVP, the person you are matched to send a gift to may well be in a different country than you. Be aware that if you choose  not  to ship internationally but are the only person in your country to join the event, you  will be matched to send a gift to someone in another country – get around this by inviting your friends – physical and virtual! A word on international sanctions and other challenges It’s impossible to run this event and ignore the spectre of international sanctions and challenges arising from conflicts that displace members of our global community. As with last year, we will be matching Russian players along with other affected countries with other players in the same country. For example, if you are based in Russia, you will only be matched with other players in Russia. Like everyone else, we’re also not certain how things will play out in the middle east right now, either. For now, we’ll leave players in Israel, Palestine, Lebanon and surrounding countries to use their own judgement and decide whether to participate. Sending and receiving gifts The “Secret” in “Secret Santa” means you don’t know who is sending you a gift… but just like every year, we’re asking you all to let you match know who you are in your card, or in note with your gift . If you’d like to stay anonymous, that is your prerogative, but more than ever, it’s about making and maintaining those connections. Don’t let the lack of wrapped gifts bother you! Please still feel free to take a photo of what you’re sending out and post it on social media along with the #EMULSIVEsanta hashtag. Welcome to the 9th annual EMULSIVE Santa film and traditional photography gift exchange! Registration this year is open until November 19th, 2023. A huge thank you to the 650-ish players in over 50 countries who came together to participate in 2022’s 8th annual EMULSIVE Santa. It was a strange event following an even stranger couple of years, but I’m still glad for it, and the very personal touches I saw being shared on social media.

With 2023’s event, our main home (Twitter / X) for the past 8 years is feeling more than a little wobbly. We’re going to try and spread things around a bit more this year and wherever you are, you should be able to see and use the #EMULSIVEsanta hashtag to keep track of things in your corner of the internet.

If you participated in any of the eight previous events, please check your email now for an invite. If not, check this year’s details and sign up sheet at the foot of the page.

Here’s what’s covered in this article:

  1. For new players: What is EMULSIVE Santa?
  2. Event timeline and sponsors
  3. Matching and wish lists
  4. A word on international sanctions and other challenges
  5. Sending and receiving gifts
  6. Don't be one of those people
  7. How to get involved
  8. It's over to you
  9. Register for EMULSIVE Santa 2023
  10. Disclaimers and terms

For new players: What is EMULSIVE Santa?

EMULSIVE Santa is the world’s largest annualfilm/traditional photography gift exchange and is now in its 9th year.

It works just like a typical Secret Santa that you might play with your family, friends, or at work but is focused purely on film and traditional photography.

Everyone’s name goes into a hat, and each person is matched randomly with another player, to whom they must send a gift worth at least US$20 (not including shipping).

Each player ends up with a match, and gift-giving goes around in an imaginary circle. It’s not a pairing, you are not giving a gift to the person who is buying you one.

Imagine this:

Event timeline and sponsors

Registration is open from today, Monday October 23rd, 2023 until Sunday, November 19th, 2023. No exceptions, I’m afraid.

Player matching is planned to be completed during the week of November 20th and players will receive details of the person they’re matched to send a gift to sometime during that week. For updates, follow the official feed over on Twitter/X: @EMULSIVEsanta.

The suggested deadline for sending gifts out is Monday December 4th, 2023 at the very latest. As with previous years, given the pressure on our global postal systems, the earlier you shop and ship, the better.

Regarding sponsors, we’ll have a few to announce in due course. For now, I’m keeping this quick, which you’ll probably appreciate is a challenge for me.

Matching and wish lists

Please be aware that depending on your event RSVP, the person you are matched to send a gift to may well be in a different country than you.

Be aware that if you choose not to ship internationally but are the only person in your country to join the event, you will be matched to send a gift to someone in another country – get around this by inviting your friends – physical and virtual!

A word on international sanctions and other challenges

It’s impossible to run this event and ignore the spectre of international sanctions and challenges arising from conflicts that displace members of our global community. As with last year, we will be matching Russian players along with other affected countries with other players in the same country. For example, if you are based in Russia, you will only be matched with other players in Russia.

Like everyone else, we’re also not certain how things will play out in the middle east right now, either. For now, we’ll leave players in Israel, Palestine, Lebanon and surrounding countries to use their own judgement and decide whether to participate.

Sending and receiving gifts

The “Secret” in “Secret Santa” means you don’t know who is sending you a gift… but just like every year, we’re asking you all to let you match know who you are in your card, or in note with your gift.

If you’d like to stay anonymous, that is your prerogative, but more than ever, it’s about making and maintaining those connections.

Don’t let the lack of wrapped gifts bother you! Please still feel free to take a photo of what you’re sending out and post it on social media along with the #EMULSIVEsanta hashtag. You can also tag EMULSIVEfilm on Twitter/X, Instagram, and Facebook, as well as EMULSIVEsanta on Twitter. There’s also the Film Photography Chat Facebook Group.

Not using those platforms? That’s ok! Please use the #EMULSIVEsanta hashtag wherever you are able to 🙏

On receiving gifts…

Please, please, please do not open your gift before Christmas Day. When you finally do, take a photo tagging the accounts above and using the #EMULSIVEsanta hashtag and anywhere else on social media.

When Christmas Day finally rolls around, post a picture of your opened gift on social media, and if your Santa has let you know who they are, go ahead and tag them.

Don’t be one of those people

EMULSIVE Santa is organised in good faith. While you can decide to remain anonymous, your actions reflect on yourself, EMULSIVE, and the good name of the analogue photography community.

Other interesting reads

As normal, any players caught no-showing will be banned from future events on EMULSIVE, and the event sponsors will also be notified.

Speaking of which.

To the dozen or so folks who truly freeloaded in 2020 (not those affected by the pretty crazy postal issues), I say this: I hope your films dry out and snap mid-roll, I hope your developer is always exhausted, and that your scans are nothing but the deepest 99.99% jet black.

There’s a special place for you in whatever version of hell you do or do not believe exists. It’s filled with people who will poke you in the eyes and other orifices with ghost peppers while rabid raccoons surgically insert a pipe between your anus and nostrils.

TLDR; get in touch if you’re having issues, please don’t be a prat.

How to get involved

Event registration is wide open, and the window is short.

You have until midnight in your timezone on Sunday, November 19th, 2023 to sign up and not a minute more. If you are a past participant, you can expect an email in your inbox already.

If you do not receive an invite in your inbox, you will need to complete the form linked below to receive your invitation link. This “double registration” system for new players was introduced back in 2017 in an attempt to reduce the number of no-shows, and along with a few other manual checks, it’s helped to reduce the no-show rate to just a few percent of players since 2019.

After you have signed up for the event, there are two things that each and every player absolutely must do. They are:

  • Set a profile picture
  • Create / update your wish list.

Sounds simple? It is. The reason for what might be considered an anally retentive request is that signing up for an event like this is simple. Forgetting to send that gift is even more so.

By setting a profile picture shows you are showing that you are engaged and interested. It takes only a little effort to complete this step, but when it comes to being matched, having one will give your Santa (the person sending you a gift), confidence that they’re matched with someone who took time out of their day to do it. As with past events, anyone who does not have a custom profile picture or wishlist set by midnight November 19th 2023 will be removed from the event without an additional warning, no exceptions.

Got questions? Send me an email once you’re registered on Elfster, and I’ll do my best to help.

It’s over to you

Sign up, get thinking and help bring joy to one of your siblings in this global film photography family of ours.

Thanks for reading,

~ Em

PS. One super important credit: a huge thanks again to @aislinn-chuahiock for the cover photo and support in pulling all this together with me. I could not do it without you!

Register for EMULSIVE Santa 2023

Please complete the Google form embedded below (or access it directly here) and grab the event invite from the confirmation page shown after you submit it.

IMPORTANT: This link is unique to you and cannot be used by anyone else. You must use that link to register on Elfster by Sunday, November 19th, 2023. Once registered, please make sure you are a member of the EMULSIVE Secret Santa 2023 gift exchange there.

Disclaimers and terms

EMULSIVE is not Elfster (the service provider used for the listing/matching). If you have any qualms about the level of your data protection, then I will have to suggest you bow out and not participate.

We’ve tested out and researched a few service providers along the way, and Elfster seemed to come out on top for the functionality they provide and what they do with data provided by their users.

We have no affiliation or commercial/personal connection with Elfster, and you use the service at your own risk. Don’t forget that I’m putting my details on there, too.

We can’t take any responsibility if anything terrible happens (they get hacked, lose your data, etc.). We’re using them in good faith, as much as you are.

Elfster is a public service, so we ask that you don’t invite participants in this event to others you may decide to create without their express consent. We’re sorry, but anyone found doing this will be excluded from entry.

Share your knowledge, story or project

The transfer of knowledge across the film photography community is the heart of EMULSIVE. You can add your support by contributing your thoughts, work, experiences and ideas to inspire the hundreds of thousands of people who read these pages each month. Check out the submission guide here.

If you like what you’re reading you can also help this passion project by heading over to the EMULSIVE Patreon page and contributing as little as a dollar a month. There’s also print and apparel over at Society 6, currently showcasing over two dozen t-shirt designs and over a dozen unique photographs available for purchase.

No, no es el Día de los Inocentes; Lomography ha anunciado hoy que reducirá el precio de la mayoría de sus películas en formato 120, en algunos casos hasta en más de un 30%.

Extraído de su comunicado de prensa:

Valoramos la espontaneidad, la rapidez y la naturaleza instintiva de la fotografía analógica. Sin embargo, hemos notado una creciente reserva dentro de la comunidad analógica en lo que respecta al distintivo y encantador formato 120.

Continúan declarando en tono de broma (?) que la película 120 es una especie en peligro de extinción, lo cual, a juzgar por lo que veo en mis tiendas locales, no está nada lejos de la realidad.

Las rebajas de precio son lo suficientemente SIGNIFICATIVAS como para escribir la palabra en mayúsculas. Aquí están sus ajustes en dólares estadounidenses. El “precio anterior” se muestra como su precio de venta al público recomendado (PVP) y puede variar de una tienda a otra:

NOTAS:

  • Me puse en contacto directamente con Lomography para confirmar que ni la Lady Grey 400 ni la Color Slide X-Pro 200 están incluidas en este ajuste de precios.
  • También puedo confirmar que esta fijación de precios pretende ser permanente y verán avisos de “OFERTA” en sus sitios web como una señal visual para llamar la atención sobre los nuevos precios. Me han informado que esperan actualizar esto a su debido tiempo.

Lomography ha estado asociada durante mucho tiempo con el sector más accesible de la fotografía analógica: equipos, películas y precios asequibles. La asequibilidad ya no es algo que se pueda decir de la gran mayoría de las películas fotográficas, y es fantástico ver a una empresa como Lomography realizar ajustes en la dirección opuesta a casi cualquier otra que se me ocurra.

A continuación, enlaces útiles:

  • Comprar películas 120 de Lomography: https://shop.lomography.com/film/120-film 
  • Comprar cámaras 120 de Lomography: https://shop.lomography.com/cameras/all?camera_filmformat=5590 

El mundo ha cambiado significativamente tras el COVID, por lo que es difícil decir si estos cambios de precio son indicativos de una tendencia mayor (a futuro) por parte de empresas como Kodak, ILFORD, Fujifilm, entre otras. También es difícil saber si estos precios son sostenibles para Lomography, pero, al menos, aplaudo el esfuerzo.

Yo también voy a salir corriendo a comprar algo de película antes de que lleguen todos ustedes 🙂

~ Em

PD: Es posible que su distribuidor local (pequeño comercio) respete o no los precios de venta al público sugeridos, actuales o nuevos, de Lomography. Probablemente también estén lidiando con la realidad del aumento de los costes, así que denles un respiro y, en el peor de los casos, busquen otro proveedor. Creo que todavía quedan algunos por ahí 😉
